articles.label: County Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47M reserve fund sits untouched as commissioners debate summer road projects
articles.dek: Three months into the fiscal year, the county has approved zero new infrastructure contracts. Staff says the bidding process is backlogged. Commissioners say they're being cautious. Residents on Scenic Highway say their potholes don't care.
brief: Escambia County has not approved any new road or infrastructure contracts since the fiscal year began in October, leaving $47 million in reserve funds unspent.
County staff cite a backlogged bidding process and staff vacancies in the Public Works department, while commissioners point to concerns about inflation and project cost overruns.
Residents in several districts, particularly along Scenic Highway and in the Ferry Pass area, have submitted dozens of road maintenance complaints that remain unaddressed.
articles.body:
The pothole on Scenic Highway near 17th Avenue is deep enough to lose a shoe in. Patricia Womack knows because her husband did, stepping out of their Camry last month after the front tire dropped into it.

"He thought he was stepping onto pavement," Womack said. "He was not."

The hole has been there since February. Womack has called the county three times. She's been told it's on a list.

Three months into Escambia County's fiscal year, that list is long and getting longer. The county has not approved a single new infrastructure contract since October 1. The $47 million sitting in reserve funds for capital projects remains untouched. And the commissioners who control that money say they're in no rush to spend it.

The money is there. The contracts are not.

Escambia County entered fiscal year 2026 with its largest reserve fund in a decade. Property tax revenues came in $12 million above projections last year. The tourism development tax exceeded forecasts. Federal infrastructure money from the 2021 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law finally cleared bureaucratic hurdles and landed in county accounts.

County Administrator Wes Moreno told commissioners in October that the county was "positioned to make significant investments in roads, drainage, and deferred maintenance."

Eight months later, none of those investments have materialized.

According to records reviewed by The Flightline, the county's Public Works department submitted seven project bids for commissioner approval between October and March. All seven were tabled. Four have since been withdrawn for "re-scoping." Three remain in limbo.

"We're being careful," District 3 Commissioner Lumon May said at the May 16 board meeting. "We've seen what happens when you rush into contracts and costs spiral. I'd rather take our time and get it right."

May did not respond to a request for comment for this story.

A department stretched thin

County staff tell a different story.

The Public Works department is currently operating with 23 vacancies out of 89 budgeted positions, according to human resources records obtained through a public records request. That includes four vacancies in the engineering division responsible for project design and bid preparation.

The department has lost eight employees since January. Three left for private-sector jobs. Two retired. Three were terminated for cause.

"We're doing more with less, and eventually that math stops working," said one current Public Works employee who requested anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. "Every project that comes back for re-scoping is another month of delay. And we don't have the people to turn them around fast."

Public Works Director Derek Burleigh declined to be interviewed but provided a written statement saying the department "remains committed to delivering quality infrastructure projects" and that "staffing challenges are being addressed through ongoing recruitment efforts."

The county's most recent job posting for a civil engineer in Public Works has been open for 147 days.

The backlog grows

Meanwhile, the county's road maintenance request system shows 1,247 open service requests as of June 1. That's up from 834 at the start of the fiscal year.

The requests range from minor—faded lane markings, overgrown rights-of-way—to serious. Forty-three requests describe potholes as "hazardous" or "dangerous." Twelve specifically mention vehicle damage. One, filed April 19, describes a sinkhole on Fairfield Drive in Ferry Pass that the submitter says has grown "from the size of a dinner plate to the size of a manhole cover."

That sinkhole remains unfilled. A county inspector visited the site on May 3 and marked it for repair. No repair has been scheduled.

District 4 Commissioner Robert Bender, whose district includes Ferry Pass, said he's aware of the backlog and frustrated by it.

"I hear from constituents every week about roads," Bender said. "I push staff. Staff says they need more resources. We've got resources sitting in reserve. But every time I try to move a project forward, I get told we need more bids, more analysis, more review."

Bender said he plans to introduce a motion at the June 20 board meeting to fast-track three specific road projects in his district. He's unsure whether he has the votes.

The caution argument

Commissioners who favor the slower approach point to recent history. In 2023, the county approved a $14 million contract for drainage improvements in the Brownsville area. The project came in $4.2 million over budget after the contractor encountered unexpected soil conditions. The county had to dip into reserves to cover the gap.

Commission Chair Jeff Bergosh has cited that project repeatedly when arguing for more rigorous bid review.

"We owe it to taxpayers to make sure every dollar is spent wisely," Bergosh said at the April board meeting. "That means doing our due diligence, even if it takes longer."

But critics argue the caution has become paralysis. County reserve funds are earning roughly 4.8 percent in interest, according to the clerk's office. Construction costs in the Pensacola market rose 6.3 percent over the past year, according to data from the Associated General Contractors of America. Every month the county waits, projects get more expensive.

"They're losing money by sitting on it," said Marcus Champagne, a retired contractor who has followed county infrastructure issues for years and frequently speaks at public comment. "You can call it caution. I call it indecision."

What's next

The June 20 board meeting will include a presentation from county staff on the project backlog. Moreno has said he will recommend prioritizing seven "shovel-ready" projects totaling $18 million. Whether commissioners will approve any of them remains unclear.

Bender said he's optimistic. May has said publicly he wants to see more cost analysis. Bergosh has not committed either way. Commissioners Steven Barry and Mike Kohler did not respond to requests for comment.

Patricia Womack doesn't much care about the internal politics. She cares about the pothole on Scenic Highway. Her husband has started wearing work boots when he gets out of the car, just in case.

"I pay taxes," Womack said. "I vote. I call when there's a problem. What else am I supposed to do?"

The county has not yet told her when the pothole will be fixed. It remains on a list.

articles.label: Feature
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's hurricane prep drill exposed communication gaps. Now they're rewriting the playbook.
articles.dek: Last month's exercise left two squadrons without evacuation orders for 90 minutes. With peak season approaching, base leadership is overhauling a notification system that dates to 2019.
brief: A May hurricane drill at NAS Pensacola revealed critical failures in the base notification system, leaving Training Air Wing Six's two squadrons without evacuation orders for 90 minutes
Base leadership has launched an overhaul of the AtHoc emergency notification system, which hasn't been significantly updated since 2019, with new protocols expected before peak hurricane season
The communication breakdown affected approximately 1,200 personnel and prompted an immediate after-action review that identified outdated contact lists and redundant notification pathways
articles.body:
At 0900 on May 14, sirens sounded across Naval Air Station Pensacola. The base's annual hurricane preparedness exercise had begun. Within minutes, most of the installation's 16,000 military and civilian personnel received text alerts on their phones, emails in their inboxes, automated calls to their desk lines.

At hangars 1440 and 1445 on the south end of the flight line, nothing came through.

The roughly 1,200 personnel assigned to Training Air Wing Six's VT-4 and VT-6 squadrons waited. They checked phones. Refreshed email. At 0947, a runner from the base operations center finally reached VT-4's duty officer with paper evacuation orders.

Ninety minutes. In a real storm, that's the difference between an orderly withdrawal and chaos.

"That's not acceptable," said Capt. Marcus Webb, NAS Pensacola's commanding officer, in an interview this week. "When we run these exercises, we're looking for exactly these kinds of failures. We found one. Now we fix it."

A system showing its age

The failure traced back to AtHoc, the Department of Defense's enterprise emergency notification platform. NAS Pensacola's instance of the system was last significantly configured in 2019, according to base spokesman Lt. Cmdr. David Reyes. Since then, organizational restructuring has rendered portions of the contact database obsolete.

Training Air Wing Six was redesignated in 2021. The squadrons moved to their current hangars in 2023. Somewhere in those transitions, the notification system's geographic and organizational targeting fell out of alignment with reality.

"The system sent alerts to where those units used to be," Reyes said. "Personnel assigned to those physical buildings weren't receiving notifications addressed to their organizational codes. And vice versa."

It's the kind of administrative drift that happens on any large installation. Phone numbers change. People transfer. Units reorganize. Without regular maintenance, the gaps compound.

The 2019 configuration came just months before Hurricane Sally struck Pensacola in September 2020, causing significant damage to the base and surrounding area. At the time, the system worked. But five years of incremental changes had degraded its reliability.

The overhaul

Webb has ordered a complete audit of the AtHoc system, with new protocols scheduled for implementation before the traditional peak of hurricane season in mid-August. The review encompasses three main areas.

First, contact verification. Every person with base access—military, civilian, dependent, contractor—will reconfirm their notification preferences and contact information through a mandatory check-in process. Those who fail to comply will have base access suspended, Reyes said.

Second, geographic targeting. The base is remapping its physical footprint within AtHoc, assigning every building a verified notification zone. Personnel will receive alerts based on both their organizational assignment and their physical location.

Third, redundancy testing. Rather than annual exercises, the base will conduct quarterly notification drills targeting random sectors. No advance warning. No waivers.

"We're going to find out if the message gets through," Webb said. "Every quarter. Every building. Until I'm satisfied."

The broader context

NAS Pensacola's communication breakdown isn't unique. A 2024 Government Accountability Office report found that 23 percent of domestic military installations had not conducted comprehensive tests of their emergency notification systems within the previous 24 months. The report cited staffing shortages and competing priorities.

Pensacola had conducted annual tests. The system still failed.

"Testing is necessary but not sufficient," said Dr. Amanda Foster, a disaster preparedness researcher at the University of West Florida. "You have to test the right things. A notification system that works perfectly for 95 percent of your personnel is still a system that fails 5 percent of your personnel."

Those margins matter in the Florida Panhandle. The region has experienced direct impacts from four named storms since 2018, including Hurricane Michael in 2018 and Hurricane Sally in 2020. Climate projections suggest the trend will continue.

For NAS Pensacola, the stakes extend beyond the installation's gates. The base houses the Naval Aviation Museum, the National Flight Academy, and multiple tenant commands. On any given day, thousands of visitors pass through. A notification failure during an actual emergency could mean civilians on base without instructions.

What comes next

The contact verification process began Monday. Personnel have until June 20 to update their information. The first unannounced quarterly drill will occur sometime before July 15, Reyes said.

Webb acknowledged the timeline is aggressive. Peak hurricane season doesn't wait.

"We got lucky in May," he said. "We found this problem during a drill, not during a storm. I don't intend to rely on luck again."

The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season began June 1. NOAA's seasonal forecast calls for above-average activity, with 14 to 21 named storms predicted. Four to seven are expected to reach major hurricane status.

Somewhere in that count, one might aim for the Panhandle. When it does, the message needs to reach every hangar.

articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: The Perdido Key condo that wasn't: How a $180M project became a parking lot and a lawsuit
articles.dek: Five years ago, developers promised 200 luxury units and a public beach access point. The land sits empty. The permits expired. And Escambia County is still waiting on $2.1 million in impact fees it may never collect.
brief: Gulf Meridian Partners obtained permits in 2021 for a 200-unit luxury condo tower on Perdido Key, promising $2.1 million in impact fees and public beach access
The project stalled after foundation work began, permits expired in 2024, and the site has sat vacant for two years while developers and county officials trade blame
Escambia County filed suit in March 2026 seeking the unpaid impact fees; Gulf Meridian countersued claiming the county's permit delays caused the project's collapse
articles.body:
The chain-link fence around the lot at 16400 Perdido Key Drive has been there so long the salt air turned it orange. Behind it, a concrete pad the size of a basketball court sits cracked and colonized by sea oats. A faded sign still promises "Azure Shores Residences — Now Pre-Leasing" with a phone number that rings to a disconnected line.

Five years ago, this 3.2-acre parcel was supposed to become the first new condominium tower on Perdido Key in over a decade. Gulf Meridian Partners, a development group registered in Delaware with offices in Destin, told county commissioners the $180 million project would bring 200 luxury units, 15 permanent jobs, and something residents had requested for years: a dedicated public beach access point with 40 parking spaces.

None of it happened.

The permits expired in December 2024. The access point was never built. And Escambia County is now suing Gulf Meridian for $2.1 million in impact fees the developer agreed to pay but never did — fees that were supposed to fund road improvements on Perdido Key Drive, already strained by tourist traffic every summer.

Gulf Meridian fired back with a countersuit in April, claiming the county's own bureaucratic delays killed the project. The developer says Escambia officials took 14 months to approve a revised stormwater plan, missing the window when construction financing was available at viable rates.

Both sides say they have the documents to prove it. Neither has produced them publicly.

The deal that wasn't

The project's origins trace to a 2020 Escambia County Commission workshop on Perdido Key development. Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes the key, had been fielding complaints for years about limited public beach access. Most of the shoreline is fronted by private condos. The handful of public access points fill up by 9 a.m. on summer weekends.

"We had residents telling us they couldn't get to their own beach," Bergosh said at the December 2020 workshop, according to meeting minutes. "If a developer wants to build out here, they need to give something back."

Gulf Meridian appeared six months later with a proposal that seemed to answer that call. The company, led by managing partner David Ashworth, presented plans for a 22-story tower with ground-floor retail, a public plaza, and the beach access point Bergosh wanted. In exchange, they sought expedited permitting and a partial waiver on impact fees.

The commission approved the project 4-1 in September 2021. Commissioner Lumon May cast the sole dissenting vote, expressing concern about traffic impacts and what he called "a lot of promises with no enforcement mechanism."

The development agreement required Gulf Meridian to complete the public access point before receiving a certificate of occupancy for any residential units. Impact fees — $2.1 million total — were due in four installments tied to construction milestones.

The first installment of $525,000 was due when vertical construction began. Gulf Meridian never paid it.

What went wrong

Permits were issued in March 2022. Site work began that May. Workers cleared vegetation, graded the lot, and poured the foundation pad that still sits there today.

Then everything stopped.

According to Gulf Meridian's countersuit, filed in Escambia County Circuit Court on April 3, 2026, the company submitted a revised stormwater management plan in June 2022 after engineers discovered the original design wouldn't meet updated state requirements for coastal construction. The filing claims the county's Development Services Department didn't approve the revision until August 2023 — 14 months later.

"By the time Escambia County issued approval, the financing terms Gulf Meridian had secured were no longer available," the countersuit states. "Interest rates had increased by more than 200 basis points. The project was no longer economically viable under the approved timeline."

The county tells a different story.

In its March 2026 complaint, Escambia officials say Gulf Meridian submitted an incomplete stormwater revision that required three rounds of corrections. The county claims it met every statutory deadline for review and that Gulf Meridian's own engineers caused the delays by failing to address technical deficiencies.

"The developer is attempting to blame the county for its own financial mismanagement," County Attorney Alison Rogers said in a statement provided to The Flightline. "Escambia County processed this application consistent with all applicable timelines. The developer simply failed to perform."

Gulf Meridian declined interview requests. A spokesperson for Ashworth emailed a one-sentence response: "We look forward to presenting the full record in court."

The money question

The $2.1 million in unpaid impact fees represents more than a contractual dispute. It's money Escambia County was counting on.

According to budget documents from fiscal year 2023, the county allocated $1.4 million of the expected Gulf Meridian fees toward a planned turn lane and traffic signal improvements at the intersection of Perdido Key Drive and River Road. That project was later scaled back and funded through other sources after it became clear the fees weren't coming.

"We had to make adjustments," said Amy Lovoy, Escambia County's budget director, in an interview. "When anticipated revenues don't materialize, you either cut the project or find money somewhere else. In this case, we did a little of both."

The turn lane was completed in 2025, but the traffic signal remains unfunded. Lovoy said the county has not written off the Gulf Meridian fees and considers them a valid debt.

Whether the county can collect is another matter. Gulf Meridian Partners appears to be a shell company with minimal assets. Florida Department of State records show the entity's registered agent is a corporate services firm in Tallahassee. Its most recent annual report, filed in February 2026, lists no officers or directors by name — only references to "managing member" designations held by other LLCs registered in Delaware.

David Ashworth, the managing partner who presented to commissioners in 2021, is also listed as principal of Ashworth Development Group, a Destin-based firm involved in several Florida Panhandle projects. It's unclear what legal relationship exists between that company and Gulf Meridian Partners. Ashworth did not respond to questions about the corporate structure.

What's next

The lawsuit and countersuit are both in the discovery phase. A case management conference is scheduled for August 14 in Pensacola.

Meanwhile, the lot at 16400 Perdido Key Drive remains what it's been for two years: an empty concrete slab behind a rusting fence. The public beach access point exists only in the 2021 development agreement, which technically remains in effect even though the permits it references have expired.

Bergosh, still the district commissioner, said he's "frustrated but not surprised" by how the project ended.

"This is what happens when you rely on private developers to deliver public benefits," Bergosh said in a phone interview. "They make promises during the approval process, and then when things go sideways, the public gets nothing. We need better tools to hold these folks accountable."

He said he plans to propose an ordinance requiring developers to post bonds or letters of credit for promised public amenities before permits are issued. Whether his colleagues will support it remains to be seen. A similar proposal failed in 2019.

May, the commissioner who voted against the project, said the outcome validated his concerns.

"I asked at the time: what happens if they don't follow through?" May said. "And here we are. Five years later, no building, no beach access, and we're spending taxpayer money on lawyers trying to collect fees we should have required up front."

The next commission discussion on development agreement reforms is scheduled for June 18. Public comment will be accepted.
